text: the presence or absence of non-pulmonary visceral metastas- es, patients with metastatic disease can be categorised into good, intermediate, and poor-risk groups.4 Consequently, there has been interest in minimising the treatment in pa- tients with good prognosis in order to reduce long-term morbidity. In such patients, 3 cycles of BEP,1,4,6,7 or 4 cy- cles of EP, may be adequate.2,4,6 The substitution of carbo- platin for cisplatin has resulted in a 10% lower relapse-free survival, and slightly reduced overall survival, and is not usually recommended,2,6 although some have reported good results with such a regimen in children.8 There is ev- idence that overall survival is improved by increased dose- intensity of etoposide and perhaps bleomycin.9 Standard management for patients with intermediate- or poor-risk disease is 4 cycles of BEP.1,4,6,7 However, less than 50% of poor-risk patients achieve a durable response and they may be offered more intensive chemotherapy such as accelerat- ed therapy, dose escalation with use of haematopoietic growth factors, or high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell support, with the aim of improving responses. So far, those intensive treatments evaluated in randomised clinical stud- ies have not proved more effective than BEP, and have of- ten been more toxic.2,3 Studies are ongoing.2 Secondary re- section of residual tumour after chemotherapy is usual.1-4 Patients who fail, or who relapse after, standard chemo- therapy have a poor prognosis, with an overall survival of only 20 to 25%.2 A common salvage regimen is cisplatin and ifosfamide with either vinblastine or paclitaxel.4,6 High-dose chemotherapy with stem cell support may also be considered.1,2,4,6,7,10 Drugs with activity as single agents in relapsed disease include paclitaxel, oxaliplatin, and gemcitabine.1,2,6,7 Seminoma is extremely sensitive to radiation, and adju- vant radiotherapy is the treatment of choice after orchidec- tomy in limited disease (stage I) and disease with low tu- mour burden (stages IIA and IIB).1-4,6,7 About three- quarters of patients have stage I disease at diagnosis and cure rates are between 95 and 100%. However, seminoma also responds very well to chemotherapy such as adjuvant single-agent carboplatin;6,7 it has been compared with ad- juvant radiotherapy for stage I disease. One study11 found that after 4 years the relapse rates were similar, but long- term follow-up was required.
